name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_Q2_1 - Charge on capacitor in steady state circuit

questiontext.text: A capacitor of \(4\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) is connected as shown in the circuit (Fig. 2.1). The internal resistance of the battery is \(0.5\ \Omega\). The amount of charge on the capacitor plates will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Capacitance of the capacitor, \(C = 4\ \mu\mathrm{F}\).
Emf of the battery, \(E = 2.5\ \mathrm{V}\).
Internal resistance of the battery, \(r = 0.5\ \Omega\).
Resistance in series with the capacitor in the top branch, \(R_{1} = 10\ \Omega\).
External resistance in the bottom parallel branch, \(R_{2} = 2\ \Omega\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The circuit is assumed to be in DC steady state, meaning the capacitor is fully charged and acts as an open circuit, so zero current flows through the capacitor branch.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Steady-state current in a closed loop with internal resistance: \(I = \frac{E}{R_{2} + r}\).
2. Terminal potential difference across the battery and parallel branch: \(V = I R_{2}\).
3. Charge stored on a capacitor: \(Q = C V\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since no current flows through the \(10\ \Omega\) resistor in steady state, the current \(I\) flows only through the loop containing the \(2.5\ \mathrm{V}\) battery and the \(2\ \Omega\) resistor:
\[I = \frac{2.5\ \mathrm{V}}{2\ \Omega + 0.5\ \Omega} = \frac{2.5}{2.5} = 1\ \mathrm{A}\]
The potential difference across the \(2\ \Omega\) resistor (and hence across the parallel capacitor branch) is:
\[V = I R_{2} = 1\ \mathrm{A} \times 2\ \Omega = 2\ \mathrm{V}\]
Because there is no current through the \(10\ \Omega\) resistor, there is no potential drop across it, so the entire \(2\ \mathrm{V}\) appears across the \(4\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) capacitor.
The charge on the capacitor plates is:
\[Q = C V = 4\ \mu\mathrm{F} \times 2\ \mathrm{V} = 8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The terminal voltage \(2\ \mathrm{V}\) is less than the emf \(2.5\ \mathrm{V}\), which is physically consistent with a potential drop \(I r = 0.5\ \mathrm{V}\) across the internal resistance. The units \(\mu\mathrm{F} \cdot \mathrm{V} = \mu\mathrm{C}\) are consistent.
Final Answer: \(8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\).

answer.text: \(4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)
\(16\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)
\(8\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_Q2_2 - Electric potential energy of released positive charge

questiontext.text: A positively charged particle is released from rest in a uniform electric field. The electric potential energy of the charge

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A charge \(q\) placed in an electric field \(\mathbf{E}\) experiences an electrostatic force \(\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{E}\). Also, the electric field always points in the direction of decreasing electrostatic potential.

Step 2: Evaluation
For a positively charged particle (\(q > 0\)), the force \(\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{E}\) acts in the same direction as the electric field \(\mathbf{E}\). Since the particle is released from rest, it accelerates and moves along the direction of the electric field.

Step 3: Application
As the positive charge moves along the electric field, the electric field does positive work on the charge, converting electric potential energy into kinetic energy. Equivalently, since the potential \(V\) decreases along the electric field and \(U = qV\) with \(q > 0\), the electric potential energy \(U\) decreases.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The electric potential energy of the charge decreases because the charge moves along the electric field.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_Q2_3 - Work done moving charge between equipotential lines

questiontext.text: Figure 2.2 shows some equipotential lines distributed in space. A charged object is moved from point A to point B.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Three different spatial distributions of equipotential lines are shown, with potentials marked at \(10\ \mathrm{V}\), \(20\ \mathrm{V}\), \(30\ \mathrm{V}\), \(40\ \mathrm{V}\), and \(50\ \mathrm{V}\). In every distribution, point A lies on the \(20\ \mathrm{V}\) equipotential line and point B lies on the \(40\ \mathrm{V}\) equipotential line.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let \(q\) be the charge of the object moved from point A to point B. The electrostatic field is conservative.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The work done in moving a charge \(q\) from potential \(V_{A}\) to potential \(V_{B}\) in an electrostatic field is:
\[W_{AB} = q (V_{B} - V_{A})\]
Because the electrostatic force is conservative, the work done depends only on the initial and final potentials and is independent of the path or the spacing of intermediate equipotential lines.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For all three equipotential distributions:
\[V_{A} = 20\ \mathrm{V}, \quad V_{B} = 40\ \mathrm{V}\]
Therefore, the potential difference is:
\[\Delta V = V_{B} - V_{A} = 40\ \mathrm{V} - 20\ \mathrm{V} = 20\ \mathrm{V}\]
Hence, the work done in each case is \(W_{AB} = 20q\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since both the charge \(q\) and the potential difference \(\Delta V = 20\ \mathrm{V}\) are identical in all three cases, the work done is identical in all three distributions.
Final Answer: The work done is the same in all three cases.

answer.text: The work done in Fig. (i) is the greatest.
The work done in Fig. (ii) is least.
The work done is the same in Fig. (i), Fig. (ii) and Fig. (iii).
The work done in Fig. (iii) is greater than Fig. (ii) but equal to that in Fig. (i).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_Q2_4 - Electric field and potential inside conducting sphere

questiontext.text:
The electrostatic potential on the surface of a charged conducting sphere is \(100\ \mathrm{V}\). Two statements are made in this regard:

\(S_{1}\): At any point inside the sphere, electric intensity is zero.

\(S_{2}\): At any point inside the sphere, the electrostatic potential is \(100\ \mathrm{V}\).

Which of the following is a correct statement?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside the volume of a conductor is zero everywhere. Furthermore, electric field is related to electrostatic potential by \(E = -\frac{dV}{dr}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Since the electric intensity inside the charged conducting sphere is zero everywhere (\(E = 0\)), the first statement \(S_{1}\) is true. Because \(E = -\frac{dV}{dr} = 0\), the electrostatic potential \(V\) must remain constant throughout the interior of the sphere.

Step 3: Application
Since the potential is continuous across the surface of the sphere and equals \(100\ \mathrm{V}\) on the surface, the constant potential at every point inside the sphere is also \(100\ \mathrm{V}\). Therefore, the second statement \(S_{2}\) is also true, and it is a direct consequence of the electric intensity being zero inside the sphere.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
\(S_{1}\) is true, \(S_{2}\) is also true, and \(S_{1}\) is the cause of \(S_{2}\).

answer.text: \(S_{1}\) is true but \(S_{2}\) is false.
Both \(S_{1}\) & \(S_{2}\) are false.
\(S_{1}\) is true, \(S_{2}\) is also true and \(S_{1}\) is the cause of \(S_{2}\).
\(S_{1}\) is true, \(S_{2}\) is also true but the statements are independent.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_Q2_5 - Equipotentials far from non-zero net charge

questiontext.text: Equipotentials at a great distance from a collection of charges whose total sum is not zero are approximately

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
At distances \(r\) much larger than the spatial extent of a localized charge distribution, the monopole term dominates the multipole expansion of the electrostatic potential if the net charge \(Q = \sum q_{i} \neq 0\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Viewed from a great distance, the entire collection of charges acts approximately as a single point charge \(Q\) located at the origin. The potential at distance \(r\) is given by \(V(r) \approx \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{Q}{r}\).

Step 3: Application
An equipotential surface satisfies \(V = \text{constant}\), which corresponds to \(r = \text{constant}\). The locus of points at a constant distance \(r\) from a point is a sphere.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Equipotentials at a great distance from a collection of charges with non-zero total charge are approximately spheres.

answer.text: spheres.
planes.
paraboloids
ellipsoids.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQI_Q2_6 - Effective dielectric constant of series dielectric blocks

questiontext.text: A parallel plate capacitor is made of two dielectric blocks in series. One of the blocks has thickness \(d_{1}\) and dielectric constant \(k_{1}\) and the other has thickness \(d_{2}\) and dielectric constant \(k_{2}\) as shown in Fig. 2.3. This arrangement can be thought as a dielectric slab of thickness \(d (= d_{1} + d_{2})\) and effective dielectric constant \(k\). The \(k\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A parallel plate capacitor of plate area \(A\) is filled with two dielectric slabs in series: the first has thickness \(d_{1}\) and dielectric constant \(k_{1}\), and the second has thickness \(d_{2}\) and dielectric constant \(k_{2}\). The total plate separation is \(d = d_{1} + d_{2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Fringing effects at the edges are neglected, so the electric field is uniform within each dielectric slab and perpendicular to the plates.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor filled with a dielectric of constant \(k\), area \(A\), and thickness \(d\): \(C = \frac{k \varepsilon_{0} A}{d}\).
2. Equivalent capacitance of two capacitors \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) in series: \(\frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{C_{1}} + \frac{1}{C_{2}}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The individual capacitances of the two dielectric blocks are:
\[C_{1} = \frac{k_{1} \varepsilon_{0} A}{d_{1}}, \quad C_{2} = \frac{k_{2} \varepsilon_{0} A}{d_{2}}\]
Since they are in series, the equivalent capacitance \(C_{\text{eq}} = \frac{k \varepsilon_{0} A}{d_{1} + d_{2}}\) satisfies:
\[\frac{d_{1} + d_{2}}{k \varepsilon_{0} A} = \frac{d_{1}}{k_{1} \varepsilon_{0} A} + \frac{d_{2}}{k_{2} \varepsilon_{0} A}\]
Cancelling \(\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{0} A}\) from both sides:
\[\frac{d_{1} + d_{2}}{k} = \frac{d_{1}}{k_{1}} + \frac{d_{2}}{k_{2}} = \frac{k_{2} d_{1} + k_{1} d_{2}}{k_{1} k_{2}}\]
Solving for \(k\) gives:
\[k = \frac{k_{1} k_{2} (d_{1} + d_{2})}{k_{1} d_{2} + k_{2} d_{1}}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The expression is dimensionless, and for equal thicknesses \(d_{1} = d_{2}\) it reduces to the harmonic mean \(\frac{2 k_{1} k_{2}}{k_{1} + k_{2}}\). (Note: In the printed source text, the denominator is written with swapped subscripts as \(k_{1} d_{1} + k_{2} d_{2}\); the matching series-combination form is \(\frac{k_{1} k_{2} (d_{1} + d_{2})}{(k_{1} d_{1} + k_{2} d_{2})}\).)
Final Answer: \(\frac{k_{1} k_{2} (d_{1} + d_{2})}{(k_{1} d_{1} + k_{2} d_{2})}\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_Q2_7 - Equipotential surfaces for uniform field along z

questiontext.text: Consider a uniform electric field in the \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) direction. The potential is a constant

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The electrostatic potential \(V\) and electric field \(\mathbf{E}\) are related by \(dV = -\mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{r}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
For a uniform electric field \(\mathbf{E} = E_{0}\hat{\mathbf{z}}\), we have:
\[dV = -(E_{0}\hat{\mathbf{z}}) \cdot (dx\,\hat{\mathbf{x}} + dy\,\hat{\mathbf{y}} + dz\,\hat{\mathbf{z}}) = -E_{0}\,dz\]
Integrating gives \(V(x, y, z) = -E_{0} z + C\), where \(C\) is a constant.

Step 3: Application
Since \(V\) depends only on \(z\) and is independent of \(x\) and \(y\), the potential is constant for any \(x\) for a given \(z\), for any \(y\) for a given \(z\), and throughout the entire \(x\text{-}y\) plane for a given \(z\). It is not constant in all space because \(V\) varies linearly with \(z\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The potential is a constant for any \(x\) for a given \(z\), for any \(y\) for a given \(z\), and on the \(x\text{-}y\) plane for a given \(z\).

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_Q2_8 - Properties of equipotential surfaces and field strength

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The magnitude of the electric field is related to the spacing between equipotential surfaces by \(E = -\frac{dV}{dr}\). For a fixed potential difference \(\Delta V\) between successive surfaces, the perpendicular spacing \(\Delta r\) is inversely proportional to the electric field strength: \(\Delta r \propto \frac{1}{E}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Because \(\Delta r \propto \frac{1}{E}\), equipotential surfaces are closer together in regions of strong electric fields than in regions of weak electric fields. They are equally spaced only when the electric field is uniform, not always.

Step 3: Application
On a charged conductor, the surface charge density \(\sigma\) is largest at sharp edges (small radius of curvature), and the electric field just outside the conductor is \(E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{0}}\). Therefore, \(E\) is large near sharp edges and near regions of large charge densities, making the equipotential surfaces more crowded in these regions.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Equipotential surfaces are closer in regions of large electric fields compared to regions of lower electric fields, more crowded near sharp edges of a conductor, and more crowded near regions of large charge densities.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_Q2_9 - Work done moving charge along an equipotential

questiontext.text: The work done to move a charge along an equipotential from A to B

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The work done in moving a unit positive charge from point A to point B in an electrostatic field is defined by the line integral \(W_{AB} = -\int_{A}^{B} \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = V_{B} - V_{A}\) (and for any charge \(q\), \(W_{AB} = q(V_{B} - V_{A})\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
Along an equipotential surface, the electric potential is constant everywhere, so \(V_{A} = V_{B}\) and \(V_{B} - V_{A} = 0\). Equivalently, the electric field \(\mathbf{E}\) is always perpendicular to the equipotential surface, so \(\mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = 0\) at every point along the path.

Step 3: Application
Thus, the work done must be defined as \(-\int_{A}^{B} \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l}\) (per unit charge) and evaluates to zero along an equipotential surface.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The work done to move a charge along an equipotential from A to B must be defined as \(-\int_{A}^{B} \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l}\) and is zero.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_Q2_10 - Electric field and charge in constant potential region

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The electric field is the negative gradient of the electrostatic potential: \(\mathbf{E} = -\nabla V\). According to Gauss's law, the net electric flux through any closed surface equals \(\frac{q_{\text{in}}}{\varepsilon_{0}}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
If the potential \(V\) is constant throughout a region, all spatial derivatives of \(V\) vanish, so the electric field \(\mathbf{E} = 0\) everywhere in that region.

Step 3: Application
Because \(\mathbf{E} = 0\) everywhere inside the region, the electric flux through any closed Gaussian surface drawn within the region is zero. By Gauss's law, this implies there can be no net charge inside the region. Furthermore, if the region is enclosed by a conductor (electrostatic shielding), placing a charge outside induces surface charges that keep the interior field zero, so the electric field inside does not necessarily change.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
In a region of constant potential, the electric field is zero and there can be no charge inside the region.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_Q2_11 - Charge redistribution between two capacitors in circuit

questiontext.text:
In the circuit shown in Fig. 2.4, initially key \(K_{1}\) is closed and key \(K_{2}\) is open. Then \(K_{1}\) is opened and \(K_{2}\) is closed (order is important). [Take \(Q_{1}'\) and \(Q_{2}'\) as charges on \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) and \(V_{1}\) and \(V_{2}\) as voltage respectively.]

Then

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Capacitors \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) are connected in a circuit with a battery of emf \(E\) and keys \(K_{1}\) and \(K_{2}\). Initially \(K_{1}\) is closed and \(K_{2}\) is open. Later \(K_{1}\) is opened and \(K_{2}\) is closed. After redistribution, the charges on \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) are \(Q_{1}'\) and \(Q_{2}'\) and their voltages are \(V_{1}\) and \(V_{2}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both capacitors are initially uncharged, and the battery and connecting wires have negligible resistance.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Charge on a capacitor: \(Q = C V\).
2. Conservation of electric charge on an isolated system of plates.
3. Parallel capacitors in electrostatic equilibrium have equal potential differences.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
When \(K_{1}\) is closed and \(K_{2}\) is open, capacitor \(C_{1}\) is charged to the battery emf \(E\), acquiring an initial charge:
\[Q = C_{1} E\]
When \(K_{1}\) is opened, the battery is disconnected, and when \(K_{2}\) is closed, \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) are connected in parallel. Charge redistributes until both capacitors reach a common potential difference:
\[V_{1} = V_{2}\]
By conservation of charge on the isolated plates:
\[Q_{1}' + Q_{2}' = Q\]
Substituting \(Q_{1}' = C_{1} V_{1}\), \(Q_{2}' = C_{2} V_{2}\), and \(Q = C_{1} E\) gives:
\[C_{1} V_{1} + C_{2} V_{2} = C_{1} E\]
Note that \(Q_{1}' = Q_{2}'\) holds only in the special case \(C_{1} = C_{2}\), not in general.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The equations \(V_{1} = V_{2}\), \(Q_{1}' + Q_{2}' = Q\), and \(C_{1} V_{1} + C_{2} V_{2} = C_{1} E\) all follow directly from parallel connection and charge conservation.
Final Answer: Charge on \(C_{1}\) gets redistributed such that \(V_{1} = V_{2}\), \(C_{1}V_{1} + C_{2}V_{2} = C_{1}E\), and \(Q_{1}' + Q_{2}' = Q\).

charge on \(C_{1}\) gets redistributed such that \(Q_{1}' = Q_{2}'\)
charge on \(C_{1}\) gets redistributed such that \(C_{1}V_{1} + C_{2}V_{2} = C_{1}E\)

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_Q2_12 - Charge distribution on conductor at non-zero potential

questiontext.text: If a conductor has a potential \(V \neq 0\) and there are no charges anywhere else outside, then

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside the conducting material (the body of the conductor) is zero. By Gauss's law, the net charge enclosed within any region where \(\mathbf{E} = 0\) is zero.

Step 2: Evaluation
Since the conductor has a non-zero potential \(V \neq 0\) (with reference potential zero at infinity) and there are no charges anywhere outside, the conductor itself must possess charges—either on its outer surface or inside a cavity within itself.

Step 3: Application
Because \(\mathbf{E} = 0\) throughout the solid conducting material, there cannot be any net charge in the body of the conductor. Any excess charge on an isolated conductor resides on its surface (or on the inner surface if a charge is placed inside a cavity).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
There must be charges on the surface or inside itself, and there cannot be any charge in the body of the conductor.

answer.text: there must be charges on the surface or inside itself.
there cannot be any charge in the body of the conductor.
there must be charges only on the surface.
there must be charges inside the surface.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_PHYSICS_MCQII_Q2_13 - Parallel plate capacitor with key closed or open

questiontext.text:
A parallel plate capacitor is connected to a battery as shown in Fig. 2.5. Consider two situations:

A: Key K is kept closed and plates of capacitors are moved apart using insulating handle.

B: Key K is opened and plates of capacitors are moved apart using insulating handle.

Choose the correct option(s).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A parallel plate capacitor of capacitance \(C\) is connected to a battery of emf \(E\) via a key \(K\). In situation A, key \(K\) remains closed while the plate separation \(d\) is increased. In situation B, key \(K\) is opened before the plate separation \(d\) is increased.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
An insulating handle is used so no charge leaks through the handle. Edge effects are neglected.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor: \(C = \frac{\varepsilon_{0} A}{d}\).
2. Charge-voltage relation: \(Q = C V\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
When the plates are moved apart, \(d\) increases, so the capacitance \(C = \frac{\varepsilon_{0} A}{d}\) decreases in both situations.
In situation A (key \(K\) closed), the capacitor stays connected to the battery, so the potential difference \(V = E\) remains constant. Since \(Q = C V\) and \(C\) decreases, the charge \(Q\) changes (decreases).
In situation B (key \(K\) opened), the capacitor is isolated from the battery, so the charge \(Q\) on the plates remains constant. Since \(V = \frac{Q}{C}\) and \(C\) decreases, the potential difference \(V\) changes (increases).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both conclusions follow directly from \(Q = C V\) under constant-\(V\) (battery connected) and constant-\(Q\) (battery disconnected) constraints.
Final Answer: In A: \(V\) remains same and hence \(Q\) changes; in B: \(Q\) remains same and hence \(V\) changes.

answer.text: In A: \(Q\) remains same but \(C\) changes.
In B: \(V\) remains same but \(C\) changes.
In A: \(V\) remains same and hence \(Q\) changes.
In B: \(Q\) remains same and hence \(V\) changes.
